# Let's chat about a vibe-coding (🪱)

![](images/module3/castle_vibe.gif){width=50%}

## Rationale

## _Fact - A:_ Coding is a gateway to lots of tools

It gives you access to...

- Thousands of specialised R packages
- Geospatial tools such as QGIS and PostGIS
- Statistical and biometrics methods that are often only available through code
- Access to database and data engineering tools

## _Fact - B:_ LLMs can write really good code (Module1) 

(_We discussed in module 1 so will not dwell on..._)

__Advantages__

- Trained on billions of lines of code, documentation, tutorials, and technical discussions
- Have "seen" solutions to many common programming problems before
- Can generate working code in seconds
- Often better at spotting syntax errors than average programmers
- Can use thousands of packages and functions that no human could memorise
- coding is very logical/systematic...(perfect for machines)


## _Fact - C:_ You have lots of potentially great ideas

![](images/module3/castle_ideas.gif){width=50%}

Coming up lots of ideas is often easy

![](images/module3/image_bike.jpg){width=40%}

But "testing riding them" (aka seeing if the idea is actually any good) can be a hurdle to ever exploring them.



![](images/module3/image_bike_uphill.jpg){width=50%}


## Given __Fact A__ and __Fact B__, why not have LLMs write code for you so you can test ride those ideas (__Fact C__)?

Using LLM to write lowers the cost of "testing riding them"

![](images/module3/image_ebike_uphill.jpg){width=50%}



## What is vibe-coding?


As with lots of terminology in the AI boom, defining vibe-coding is a bit nebulous. Different people (and bots!) use the term differently. For our purposes, let's keep it simple:

__Vibe-coding is a workflow where you describe what you want in natural language, an LLM writes the code, and you iteratively refine the result until you achieve the desired outcome in a reproducible way.__


![](images/module3/image_vibe_coding.jpg){width=40%}


## Caveats with vibe-coding

Vibe-coding can be incredibly productive, but it comes with risks...

- failing into the trap of intellectual laziness
- accept incorrect results in which is the logic does not make sense
- use inappropriate statistical or analytical methods

![](images/module3/image_ebike_cliff.jpg){width=50%}


# Implementing a vibe-coding workflow

## Rationale

Some attributes of a good workflow for vibe-coding...

- reproducible
- makes it efficient to review the code and outputs
- aligns with the coding skills and workflow that are already in-house (@ARI)
- leverages proven workflows

Here, we will implement vibe-coding within Rstudio environment (which we have presented previously in our workshops😁)

# Copilot Approach (🐒,  🪱)

Currently all ARI staff have access to Microsoft Copilot (Basic)[^1], so that is our starting point when it comes to vibe coding.

[^1]: Some people have access to Copilot Professional, which may perform better than Copilot Basic in these tasks.

Vibe-coding with a Chatbot LLM (like Copilot) is effectively like having a conversation with someone who has read lots of stuff, so may appear knowledgable, but does not understand the topic you are going to discuss with them. Add to that they are often trying to be helpful and positive and that means that they are not always trustworthy, as they can hallucinate when giving an answer it thinks you want. So, they can be useful as sounding board and help with tasks, but you need to be aware that currently, they may unintentionally(?) mislead you.

A good starting point for any project is to plan what you are wanting to do before you start doing. This can help you define your problem and reduce the number of unproductive paths you take on the way to your solution. Let us start by using Copilot to help us devise and clarify a plan of attack for our project. Note, that as well as text, we can add [certain types of files](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365-copilot/file-formats-supported-by-microsoft-365-copilot) into the prompt window that Copilot can review and help us with our task. So, as well as the text below, we will add the final map from the QGIS workshop as a reference and the summary data of the locations (Copilot didn't like the GIS data in the .gpkg format).

> I need to create a png map using an R workflow. I have a graph attached (qgis_goal.png) that I want you to replicate. I first want to create a plan that we argue on to create similar map output (to be stored in 'figures/rmap.png') and all points will be found in the attached vmfrp_wallpolla_veg.csv (that is stored in `data/spatial/vmfrp_wallpolla_veg.gpkg` for the code). A basemap and Victorian layer will be needed to be found. I need to use the VIC font and the batlow colour scheme from the scico package. During the planning stage, do not guess what I want but rather ask me explicitly.

Then, it should start the process of walking you through a plan of attack for making the map. That should including asking you to make some choices about options and clarifying some uncertainties. Once you and Copilot are happy that you have a plan, then you can ask it to help you impliment that plan. That will include generating the code that you will require to produce the maps in a suitable format. Once you have that code, you can copy and paste it into R and then ask Copilot to help fix any issues. This will then become an iterative process of you asking for help (as needed) to update the code so that it produces the desired outcome. Be aware that during this back-and-forth there may be some context rot[^2].

[^2]: Context rot is when the LLM starts to lose track of the conversation as it goes on for a while. It is also called context drift, and can bepart of the "Lost in the Middle" problem.

I will note here, that in my experiment with Copilot to generate the map I assumed I had no real experience with coding in R, and relied on it to code everything. It did seem to struggle with fonts and the location of the insets. I suspect that Copilot is not optimised for coding, and that a different LLM could perform differently if that was your chatbot. However, I did expereince it hallucinating functions, changing the names of objects and referencing a website with URL that included "/..." as it was not sure which map I was after, rather than asking.

### Step 2: Use plan mode

Before diving into getting the spatial code, you need to have an idea/plan of what you want the `Agent` to do.  The 'plan mode' can be useful for this. 


<div style="background-color:#dbeafe; padding:1em; border:1px solid #93c5fd; border-radius:6px;">

__PROMPT__

_/plan (sets to plan mode)_

I need to create a png map using an R workflow.  I have a graph (figures/qgis_goal.png) that I want you to replicate.  I first want to create a plan that we argue on to create similar map output ('figures/rmap.png') and all points will be `data/spatial/vmfrp_wallpolla_veg.gpkg`.  A basemap and Victorian layer will be needed to be found.  See `.posit/AGENTS.MD` '.posit/spatial_analyst/' skill to guide workflow approach.  During the planning stage, do not guess what I want but rather ask me explicitly.  Save the plan as PLAN.MD in base directory.

</div>

### Summary table of insights...

|Rank| Model | \~Cost | Thoughts |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
|1| Claude Sonnet (1.0x)  | $3.30 | More expensive model but it viewed the png file with no issues and just needed to ask a few questions.  It was able to evaluate how well it had done and fix several components |
|1-2nd attempt| GLM 5.3 (0.6x) | $1.20 | On second attempt (a few days later), it was able to create a subagent as a viewer.  It re-iterated by itself to really get final map (no prompting from me).  Did it learn from previous attempt?? |
|3| Kimi (0.9x)    | $4.66 | First draft was very close. It seemed to evaluate along the way, so the final revision prompt not as needed.   |
|4-1st attempt| GLM 5.3 (0.6x) | $1.00 | First try, not able to "view" the png so had to try to walk it through via queries.  Output was pretty poor. |
|4| Claude Haiku (0.4x)  | $0.72 | Least expensive model I tried. Clunkier in how its ask question.  Did not suggest/recommend approaches. Created 6 script files|

# Coming back to vibe-coding idea

## Some final thoughts

_Disclaimer: This is us free-thinking in real time during a paradign shift. Feel free to disagree or contribute your own thoughts._

### Resist intellectual laziness

This is not a flippant statement.

As AI tools become more capable, there is a risk that we outsource not only the coding, but also the thinking.

Contributing factors:

- We are increasingly time-stressed.
- Projects often have unrealistic deadlines.
- Vibe-coding can create psychological distance from the underlying problem.
- Modern digital platforms reward speed, visibility, and confidence more than deep understanding.
- AI can produce plausible outputs that reduce the incentive to question assumptions or verify results.

__Key message:__ The danger is not that AI writes code. The danger is that we stop engaging critically with the problem we are trying to solve.


### Reviewing the code

- Despite the temptation, we are going to need to be disciplined about reading the code and ensure 
that we understand exactly what it is doing.

- Not all code requires the same level of assessment (importing data vs ggplot vs statistical analysis)

- Learning how to <span style="color: blue;">QC/QA your code and outputs will increase in importance</span>

- As noted, I have a STYLE.MD guide that writes the code in my style.  That helps me review/evaluate the code quicker.


### Learning from vibe-coding

- New approaches to tackling a problem (plan mode)

- Reading the code that the Agent wrote introduced me to new functions/approaches to making new maps


### Beyond spatial data

- Obviously, __vibe-coding is not restricted to spatial data__ and you can implement the same approach to other type of data.


### Homogensing workflow (the future)

An emerging question that we are wondering about (and we mentioned in module 1...sorry to dwell) is what does this mean for how we tackle these steps in the future and our workflows.  

How homogenized do our workflows become?  

  - Standardised ARI STYLE.MD, WOKFLOW.MD, and set of SKILLS.MD files/folders.  
  - Do we have a project folder that has a similar structure so both humans and a local LLM that has been trained on our workflow can easily understand it, revise, and QC it?


All of this seems apt given all the discussion on templates/standardisation
